note: The Swiss Army knife of Japan: calls a waiter over, apologizes when squeezing past someone on the train, and says 'thank you for going out of your way' when someone holds an elevator or picks up something you dropped.

kanji: ありがとうございます
kana: ありがとうございます
note: Your default polite thank-you with clerks, neighbors, and staff. With close friends or family, drop ございます and just say ありがとう.

english: Please (when asking for or ordering something)
note: Lit. 'I make a request.' Use this when ordering food, asking for a service, or handing forms over—unlike ください ('please give me'), お願いします feels collaborative rather than demanding.

english: Nice to meet you / Looking forward to working together
kanji: よろしくお願いします
kana: よろしくおねがいします
note: Lit. 'Please treat me favorably.' Used when meeting a new neighbor, starting a project, or wrapping up a request ('Thanks in advance!'). With friends: just よろしく！

english: It's okay / I'm fine / No, thank you
note: Lit. 'Strong and secure.' Watch out at the konbini: locals use 大丈夫です to mean 'No bag/receipt needed,' but some clerks take it as 'Yes, that's fine'—use いりません when you want zero ambiguity.
Warmer and more personal than すみません—use ごめんなさい (or casual ごめん！) with friends, partners, and family, and save すみません for strangers and staff.

kanji: ちょっと待ってください
kana: ちょっとまってください
note: Handy at the door with a delivery driver or at a register while you dig for coins. With friends, drop ください and just say ちょっと待って！

english: One more time, please (could you repeat that?)
kanji: もう一度お願いします
kana: もういちどおねがいします
note: Polite and natural with clerks or staff when you miss a fast question. With friends in casual conversation, say もう一回！ (Mou ikkai!).

kanji: もう少しゆっくりお願いします
kana: もうすこしゆっくりおねがいします
note: Your best friend when a clerk or station attendant fires off rapid-fire keigo. ゆっくり is also the root of ごゆっくりどうぞ ('Take your time!').
Plug any word you just heard right in front of it: 「[Word]」ってどういう意味ですか？ ('What does [Word] mean?').
Says 'I understand' after someone gives you directions or instructions. Don't confuse it with 知ってます ('I already knew that fact').

english: I'm not sure / I don't quite know
kanji: ちょっとわかりません
kana: ちょっとわかりません
note: Adding ちょっと ('a little') softens 'I don't know / understand' so it never sounds blunt or unhelpful.

kana: にほんご、べんきょうちゅうです
note: 中 (-chū) means 'right in the middle of' (like 営業中 = open for business). Saying this immediately makes locals slow down and root for you.

kana: だいじょうぶ、きにしないで
note: Lit. 'Don't put it on your mind/spirit (気).' The go-to casual way to wave off a friend's apology.

english: You saved me! / That was a huge help!
note: Lit. 'I was rescued!' Way warmer and more grateful than a generic ありがとうございます when someone holds a door, explains a form, or covers for you.

kana: えいご、だいじょうぶですか？
note: If they reply 「英語はちょっと…」 (trailing off on chotto), that's a polite soft 'No, I can't really speak English.'

english: Could you write that down for me?
note: Lifesaver at clinics, ward offices, or restaurants when you can't catch a spoken kanji name, address, or appointment time.

english: Could you show / tell me this?
kana: これ、おしえてください
note: 教える means both 'to teach' and 'to tell/show' (like asking for the Wi-Fi password or how a ticket machine works).

english: Thanks for your hard work! / Hey (work & delivery)
note: Lit. 'You must be tired.' Said to coworkers, building staff, and delivery drivers—and when clinking first beers after work (お疲れ！). Never say it to store clerks, and never say ご苦労様 to someone senior.

kana: おさきにしつれいします
note: Said when leaving work, a gym class, or a group hangout before everyone else—acknowledges that others are still working or hanging out.

english: Excuse me for coming in (stepping into a home)
note: Lit. 'I'm going to be in your way (邪魔).' Say it the exact moment you step across someone's doorway or into a private room.
Keep お and です with neighbors, hairdressers, and regular bartenders; drop both for close friends (久しぶり！).

english: Please don't push yourself too hard / Take it easy
kanji: 無理しないでくださいね
kana: むりしないでくださいね
note: Lit. 'Please don't do the impossible (無理).' Locals say this constantly when someone is working late, feeling under the weather, or out in summer heat.
The everyday spoken cousin of ケセラセラ ('Que sera, sera')—used to calm a friend down when plans get messy.

english: Oh, that's what you mean! / Aha, I get it now!
note: The 'lightbulb moment' reaction when a confusing rule, joke, or backstory finally clicks.
Clearer than 大丈夫です at the konbini—plastic bags cost ¥3–¥5 now, so clerks ask every time.

kana: ふくろ、おねがいします
note: Say this right after the clerk scans your items (or when they ask レジ袋はご利用ですか？).

kana: あたため、おねがいします
note: Konbini staff will always ask if you want bento or onigiri warmed up—just say this and they'll pop it in the microwave.

kana: おはし、おねがいします
note: Even if you didn't catch their question, hearing お箸 (o-hashi) means they're offering free disposable chopsticks.

kana: レシート、だいじょうぶです
note: Tells the clerk you don't need the paper receipt—or say レシートください if you want to keep it.

english: I don't have a point card
kanji: ポイントカード、ないです
kana: ポイントカード、ないです
note: Every konbini and drugstore asks for a point card (Ponta, d-Point, V-Point). This shuts it down politely in one second.
Great icebreaker at counter bars, ramen shops, or bakeries—chefs love pointing out their pride-and-joy dish.
Point at the pastry or menu photo and swap the counter: ひとつ (1), ふたつ (2), みっつ (3).

kanji: いつもの、お願いします
kana: いつもの、おねがいします
note: The badge of becoming a neighborhood regular—save this for the coffee shop or bakery where they already know your order.
Waitstaff usually bring free water automatically, but at tiny counter spots or izakayas you'll want to ask for it.

english: Do you have an English menu?
kanji: 英語メニュー、ありますか？
kana: えいごメニュー、ありますか？
note: Handy at busy spots—even if they don't have one, they'll often bring a photo menu or point out favorites.
Say this right as you walk in, followed by your name (e.g., デイビッドです).

english: Table for two / Two of us
note: Counter for people: ひとり (1), ふたり (2), さんにん (3), よにん (4). Never say しにん for 4—it sounds like 'dead person'!

kana: ちゅうもん、いいですか？
note: Say すみません first to flag down staff, then drop this when you're ready to order.

kanji: これと同じの、ください
kana: これとおなじの、ください
note: Lifesaver when you spot someone else's delicious dish at the counter or point to a photo on the wall.

kanji: テイクアウトで、お願いします
kana: テイクアウトで、おねがいします
note: Tax is actually 8% for takeout vs. 10% for dining in (店内で / tennai de), which is why cafes always ask!

kanji: 卵アレルギーがあります
kana: たまごアレルギーがあります
note: Swap 卵 (egg) for えび (shrimp), ピーナッツ (peanuts), or 小麦 (wheat) so kitchens take it seriously.

kana: おかいけい、おねがいします
note: Many local spots don't bring the check to your table—say this to your server or walk up to the register.
More places take cards now, though tiny ramen shops and cash-only izakayas still exist—always smart to check.
Quick heads-up check before ordering at a cozy neighborhood spot or food stall.

kana: べつべつで、できますか？
note: Some busy izakayas won't split checks at the register (they'll ask you to pay together), so it's polite to ask first.
割り勘 (warikan) is splitting evenly—super common among friends after an izakaya night.
めっちゃ started in Kansai (Osaka) slang and is now used all over Japan by friends—super natural reaction!
A warm goodbye to a local shopkeeper or barista—tells them you genuinely liked the place.
Say this as you walk out to the staff or the Master (the chef/owner behind the counter)—and especially to whoever paid for your food or drinks, even by text the next day.

kanji: 置き配で、お願いします
kana: おきはいで、おねがいします
note: 置き配 (okihai) is the magic word for contactless delivery at your door—standard with Amazon, Yamato, and Uber Eats.
Buzz back on the apartment intercom right away so the courier doesn't walk off and leave a missed-delivery slip.

english: In front of the door, please
kanji: 玄関の前に、お願いします
kana: げんかんのまえに、おねがいします
note: Tells the delivery driver exactly where to set the box if you can't come to the door.

kanji: 宅配ボックス、ありますか？
kana: たくはいボックス、ありますか？
note: Many Japanese apartments have shared metal parcel lockers in the lobby—handy when moving in or ordering deliveries.

kana: さいはいたつ、おねがいします
note: If you get a pink/white 不在票 (missed-delivery slip) in your mailbox, you can scan its QR code or call for redelivery.
Japanese neighborhoods are strict about trash pickup spots and days—asking a neighbor early on earns instant goodwill.

kanji: これ、燃えるゴミですか？
kana: これ、もえるゴミですか？
note: Trash splits into 燃えるゴミ (burnable), 燃えないゴミ (non-burnable), and 資源ゴミ (recyclables)—each has its own day.
Said to neighbors and coworkers in the morning—and also used at any hour by restaurant/bar staff starting their shift!
Daytime hello (roughly 10am–5pm). Note: you don't say こんにちは to close family or people you already greeted earlier.
Evening greeting once it gets dark—great when passing neighbors on your way home from the station.

kana: きょうもあついですね
note: Japan's #1 neighborhood small talk from June to September. Add ね at the end to invite agreement.
The autumn/winter equivalent—literally 'It has become cold, hasn't it?'
Easy elevator or apartment-entrance small talk when everyone is shaking out wet umbrellas.
A warm 'Watch out / Take care!' when someone is heading out in bad weather or walking home late.

english: I'm heading out! ('I'll go and come back')
note: Said when leaving home or the office. It literally means 'I'll go and come back'—a tiny daily promise that you'll return safely.

english: Have a good one! ('Go and come back safe')
note: The warm reply to 行ってきます when a family member, partner, or coworker heads out the door.
Short for ただいま帰りました ('I have just now returned'). Said the moment you walk back through your front door.
The automatic warm reply to ただいま—also used by bartenders and regulars at your neighborhood izakaya!
Said with prayer hands 🙏 right before your first bite. Since it literally means 'I humbly receive,' you also say it when taking a snack or gift someone hands you.

english: I'm stepping out for a bit
kanji: ちょっと出かけてきます
kana: ちょっとでかけてきます
note: Polite heads-up to a roommate, host family, or partner when you're just popping out to the konbini or for a walk.

kana: まだとどいてないです
note: Handy when checking with a roommate, reception, or support about a package or mail.
Super versatile check when signing a form, sorting trash, or placing something down.
Polite 'Either works for me'—drop to どっちでもいいよ with friends.

kanji: いつもありがとうございます
kana: いつもありがとうございます

beats.jp: ありがとうございます
beats.kana: ありがとうございます

note: The gold-standard greeting for your building superintendent, regular cafe barista, or local shop owner.

english: See you next time / Please help me again
note: Warm sign-off at a clinic, salon, or repair shop—literally 'Please take care of me again next time.'
The most natural casual check-in with a friend—way more common than textbook お元気ですか？.

english: What have you been up to lately?
note: Great opener when catching up with someone you haven't texted or seen in a few weeks.
Quick, warm 'You good?'—with people you don't know well, use お元気ですか？ instead.
Upbeat casual reply—swap だ to です (元気です！) in polite settings.
The classic casual 'Same old / Not much' when someone asks what you've been up to.
Relatable answer when you've been grinding at work all week.
Literally 'Finally settled down'—what locals actually say when a busy stretch at work or moving house wraps up.

kana: いえでゴロゴロしてた
note: ゴロゴロ is iconic Japanese sound-symbolism for rolling around at home doing absolutely nothing.
Soft, natural way to tell a friend you're wiped out—works as a gentle hint to head home early.
The universal friend opener right before you tell a funny story or drop some gossip.
Immediate follow-up when a friend looks shocked, stressed, or says 'Hey, listen to this!'

english: So glad we got to talk!
note: Warm wrap-up after catching up with someone over coffee or a long phone call.
Said right as you're parting ways after hanging out—add です (楽しかったです) if being polite.
Sweet, casual way to say 'Let's definitely hang out again!' without locking in a specific date yet.
Almost always means 'Text me on LINE!'—LINE is how everyone in Japan stays in touch.
Use this when you're heading off and will message them later with details or photos.
For birthdays, promotions, engagements, or passing a test—add ございます for formal situations.
Said whenever someone has a cold, is injured, or mentions they're not feeling well.
Cheering someone on before an exam, interview, or busy shift—add ください to make it polite.
Encouraging agreement when a friend pitches an idea, outfit, or travel plan.
Easy way to bounce the decision back to a friend when picking a restaurant or plan.

kana: ちょっときゅうけいしよう
note: Great during a long walk, shopping trip, or study session.
Drinking (飲み) is Japan's main social glue—works for beers at an izakaya or a casual bar.
Wait until *everyone* at the table has their drink before clinking glasses and shouting 乾杯！

kana: きをつけてかえってね
note: Warm goodbye when a friend is heading to the train station at night.
Japan's #1 conversational reaction—shows you're listening and taking in new info. Say そうなんですね in polite situations.

english: Oh, is that so! / I see
note: The polite, natural cousin of そうなんだ！—much smoother than なるほどですね, which can sound slightly stiff to elders.
Drawn-out 'Oh, really? Interesting!'—Japanese conversations rely on constant little reactions like this.
Light, natural 'For real?'—keeps the other person talking.
High-energy reaction when a friend drops surprising news. Keep マジで for friends, not bosses or elders.
Playful disbelief ('You're kidding me!')—never literally accusing them of lying.
Instant empathy ('I feel that so hard'). Add 超 (chou) in front—超わかる！—for extra emphasis with friends.
Thoughtful 'True, good point!'—works great when someone makes an observation you hadn't considered.
Youth/millennial slang for '100% / Preach!'—save it for friends around your age.
Friendly envy when someone tells you about a trip, bonus, or great meal.
Polite, warm enthusiasm—great with coworkers, neighbors, and acquaintances.
All-purpose praise for food, views, stories, or someone's skill—add ですね to make it polite.
Means both 'Whoa, amazing!' and 'Oh no, that's bad!'—tone tells you which one.
Casual slang for 'That cracks me up!'—from ウケる (to be well-received / hit the funny bone).
Use なるほど with peers when something clicks—avoid adding ですね with bosses or older folks.
Polite 'Right?! I knew it!'—creates instant shared agreement.
Soft, casual 'Probably / I'd guess so.'
Neutral 'Hard to say / I wonder' when neither of you is sure.

english: Speaking of which... / By the way...
note: Smooth topic-changer ('Oh, speaking of that...') when something reminds you of another story.
Super common conversational pivot ('Or actually... / Wait, I mean...')—locals drop this constantly.
Relaxed shrug ('Eh, whatever, it's fine') when a tiny thing doesn't go as planned.
Casual 'Something like that / Pretty much'—handy when summarizing a vibe or story.

english: I don't mind / Sure, whatever works
note: Notice 別に (betsu ni) sounds grumpy alone, but 別にいいよ means 'I don't mind at all, either way is fine!'

english: Something feels off / Not quite right
note: Gentle way to say 'Hmm, something feels slightly off' about an outfit, food, or vibe without sounding harsh.
Warm compliment when you and a friend share the exact same taste or sense of humor.

kana: こんしゅうきんよう、あいてる？
note: Swap 金曜 (Friday) for 土曜 (Saturday) or 日曜 (Sunday) to check if a friend is free.
Super open-ended—lets your friend suggest the day or time that works best for them.
Used when deciding on a restaurant, cafe, or meetup spot.

english: What time should we make it?
note: Natural 1-on-1 way to lock in a time—way less stiff than textbook 何時に会いますか？.
Swap 渋谷 for any neighborhood or station (新宿, 梅田, 難波) to float an idea.
Cleanest way to seal a meetup time in a LINE chat or on the phone.

kana: こんど、いっしょにいこう
note: Watch the vibe: sometimes genuine, sometimes a polite brush-off unless someone actually suggests a date!

english: Let's go for the first time in a while!
kana: ひさしぶりにいこうよ
note: Great for hitting up an old favorite ramen shop or izakaya you haven't visited in months.
Classic LINE text when you arrive at the station exit and can't spot your friend yet.
Quick reassuring text when you're 2–3 minutes away.

english: Looks like I'll be a bit late
note: Say this before you're actually late—add ごめん！ in front if you're stuck on a delayed train.

english: Go ahead and head inside first!
note: Tells your friend to grab a table or order a drink without waiting for you outside in the cold/heat.
Warm closing line on LINE right after locking in plans.

english: Can we move / push back the plan?
note: Handy when work runs late and you need to push dinner back 30 minutes or move it to another day.
Smooth way to say 'Friday doesn't work, but Saturday I'm open!'

english: Today is a bit tough... (= No, I can't today)
note: Classic Japanese soft 'no'—trailing off on ちょっと… means 'I can't make it today' without saying No directly.
Friendly way to wrap up a raincheck—just notice if nobody picks a new day, it might stay a raincheck!
Famous Japanese soft 'no'—often means 'probably not, don't wait up for me,' though sometimes people do show up.
Polite brush-off at a store or sales counter when you don't want to buy something right now.

english: Might be a bit tough / tight
kana: ちょっときびしいかも
note: Natural way to say 'Oof, that schedule/budget/deadline might be tough' without sounding harsh.
Playful 'I'm tapped out!' when you're stuffed, exhausted, or laughing too hard.

english: Does it look okay? / You good?
note: Checking in on a friend—'Looking good? Think you'll make it?'
Use when a friend suggests a time or price that works out perfectly for you.
Easygoing 'I'm flexible whenever!'
Casual, everyday goodbye with friends—you'll hear じゃあね and またね constantly.

english: What are you obsessed with lately?
note: ハマる means 'to fall into / get hooked on'—the best question to get a friend talking about their latest obsession.
Swap サウナ for コーヒー, キャンプ, or any hobby—めっちゃ makes it sound genuinely enthusiastic.
Men often swap 私 (watashi) for 俺も好き！ (ore mo suki!) in casual male speech.
Easy conversation starter—swap 映画 (movie) for アニメ, ドラマ, or 新しいカフェ.
Quick ping-pong reply that invites your friend to tell you if it's worth watching.

kana: めっちゃおもしろかった！
note: Note: 面白い means both 'funny' and 'interesting/really good' (for books, movies, and people!).
Casual way to hype up a restaurant, app, or spot you love.
Always say 一回 (ikkai), never 一度 (ichido), when telling a friend 'Just try it once!'
The ultimate compliment for spicy ramen, natto, or a hot sauna—literally 'it becomes a habit!'
Polite version for staff or shrines: 写真、撮ってもいいですか？.
きれい covers both 'pretty/beautiful' AND 'clean/tidy'—handy for views, food plating, and apartments.
Drop this at a mountain lookout, rooftop bar, or coastal train window.
Thoughtful way to dodge sweeping generalizations ('Do Japanese people like X?' → 'Depends on the person!').
Handy when someone asks 'Can you do X?' or 'How much is Y?' and the answer varies.

english: That works! / I'm down for that!
note: Casual thumbs-up ('That's a solid option / I'm down!')—used a lot when picking food or plans.

english: No way / That's a no from me
note: Playful thumbs-down ('Hard pass / No way!') among friends.

english: It is what it is / Nothing we can do
note: Everyday version of 'It is what it is'—good for missed trains or sudden rain, not for comforting someone's big loss.
Warm thing to say out loud at a concert, trip, or great restaurant—makes whoever invited you feel awesome.
おごり means 'my treat!'—expect your friend to say いいの？ありがとう！ or insist on paying next time.
Literally 'my stomach became empty'—the universal casual 'I'm starving!'
Say this after a huge meal—add です (お腹いっぱいです) at a host's house so they stop piling food on your plate!
Literally 'my throat got dry'—said when you need water or a cold beer.
Honest casual sigh around 3pm or late at night.
Reassuring 'Doesn't bother me at all!' when someone worries about noise, seating, or a small mess.
Pure enthusiasm ('The best!')—for a cold beer after work, an onsen, or a weekend trip.
-ちゃった is the casual contraction of -てしまった ('accidentally did it / oops'). Super common in daily speech!
Soft, natural 'Oops, I lost it...' when talking to a friend.
Use 壊れました (kowaremashita) when reporting a broken AC or lock to your landlord.

english: I made a mistake / Got the wrong one
note: Polite 'Sorry, I messed up / picked the wrong one'—great at ticket machines or counters.

kana: ちょっとこまってます
note: Magic opener at a ward office, bank, or train station—immediately signals you need a hand.

kanji: どうすればいいですか？
kana: どうすればいいですか？
note: Direct and polite when you're stuck on a form, missed a train, or broke something.
Essential for calling building maintenance or hotel reception.

kanji: エアコン、効かないです
kana: エアコン、きかないです
note: 効かない (kikanai) literally means 'isn't having an effect'—locals use it for AC, heaters, and medicine!
For your landlord, building manager, or local police box (交番 / kouban).
Japan has an amazing lost-and-found culture—report it at the nearest 交番 (police box) or station office right away.

english: I left my phone behind / forgot my phone
kana: けいたい、わすれました
note: 携帯 (keitai) is short for mobile phone—also called スマホ (sumaho) for smartphone.

kana: ワイファイ、つながらないです
note: Handy at cafes, hotels, and coworking spaces.

english: Can I charge my phone here?
kana: じゅうでん、できますか？
note: Many cafes and fast-food counters have outlets—always polite to ask first.

kanji: トイレットペーパー、ないです
kana: トイレットペーパー、ないです
note: Simple, clear heads-up to restaurant or store staff.
Casual 'Oops, got it stained/dirty'—for coffee spills on a shirt.

english: I think I might have dropped it
note: かも is short for かもしれない ('maybe / might have')—super natural spoken Japanese.
Polite 'I can't seem to find it' when asking store staff or lost-and-found.

english: I didn't make it in time!
note: When you just missed the last train or a store closing time.
Polite way to report loud construction, neighbors, or a noisy hotel room.

kana: へんなにおいがします
note: Useful for reporting a gas smell, weird fridge odor, or burning smell to building staff.

kana: しゅうり、おねがいします
note: Direct request at a shoe shop, bike shop, phone store, or building management.
Keep your receipt (レシート)—Japanese stores are strict about receipts for exchanges!

kanji: キャンセルしたいです
kana: キャンセルしたいです
note: Clear and polite at a restaurant, salon, or hotel counter.
Relieved 'It's fixed!'—works for Wi-Fi, appliances, or a sprained ankle.
Clear emergency cry for help—save it for real emergencies.
Simply point to your throat, tooth, knee, or back and say this—works at any clinic or pharmacy.
More natural in everyday speech than textbook 頭痛がします.
Clear, direct way to tell a doctor or friend your stomach hurts.
First sign of a cold—pharmacists will point you right to throat lozenges or sprays.

english: I feel a cold coming on
note: 気味 (-gimi) means 'a touch of / starting to feel like'—also works in 疲れ気味 (a bit run down).
っぽい (-ppoi) means '-ish'—so 熱っぽい means 'feverish' even before you check a thermometer.
Important distinction: 気分が悪い means physically nauseous/dizzy (not 'in a bad mood'!).
Clear way to tell a doctor or friend you feel lightheaded/dizzy.
Helpful at drugstores so they don't accidentally give you a general cold pill when you just need cough syrup.
Doctors always ask いつからですか？ ('Since when?')—swap 昨日 for 一昨日 (day before yesterday) or 先週 (last week).

kana: やっきょく、どこですか？
note: In Japan, clinics don't hand you pills—they give you a paper prescription to take to a nearby 薬局 (pharmacy).
Great at a drugstore (ドラッグストア) when you want over-the-counter relief.

kana: しょほうせん、おねがいします
note: Hand over your clinic paper + insurance card at the pharmacy counter with this.
Japanese cold/allergy meds often cause strong drowsiness—smart to check before driving or working!
Japanese medicine packets print 食後 (after meals) or 食前 (before meals)—good to double-check.

kana: いちにちなんかいですか？
note: Quick check on dosage (e.g., 一日三回 = 3 times a day).

english: I have my health insurance card
kana: ほけんしょう、もってます
note: Japanese National Health Insurance (保険証) covers 70% of clinic & prescription costs—always bring it!
Clinic receptionists always ask 初診ですか？ ('First visit?')—just reply はい、初めてです.

kanji: アレルギーがあります
kana: アレルギーがあります
note: Always mention drug or food allergies before a doctor prescribes anything.

english: I have hay fever / seasonal allergies
note: Cedar pollen (スギ花粉) hits hard every spring in Japan—mentioning 花粉症 gets instant sympathy everywhere!

english: I'm going to rest / take the day off
note: Text or say this when taking a sick day or stepping out to rest.

english: I'm going to the doctor / clinic
kana: びょういんにいきます
note: Note: 病院 covers both big hospitals and neighborhood clinics in everyday speech.
Warm update to friends or coworkers after recovering from a cold.

kana: もうだいじょうぶです
note: Reassures people who were worried about you ('I'm totally fine now!').

kana: きゅうきゅうしゃ、おねがいします！
note: Dial 119 in Japan for an ambulance or fire (110 is police).

english: How do I get to the station?
kanji: 駅までどう行きますか？
kana: えきまでどういきますか？
note: Simple, clear way to ask any passerby or shopkeeper for directions to the nearest station.

english: Does this train go to Tokyo?
kanji: これ、東京に行きますか？
kana: これ、とうきょうにいきますか？
note: Essential before hopping on an express train or local bus so you don't end up 3 towns over!
番線 (-bansen) is the track/platform number—super fast to ask a station attendant.
Checks whether your train goes direct or if you need to switch lines.

english: What time is the last train?
kana: しゅうでん、なんじですか？
note: 終電 (shūden) is the dreaded last train (usually around midnight)—miss it and it's taxi or karaoke till 5am!

english: I'm getting off at the next stop
note: Say すみません、次で降ります to politely part the crowd before the doors open.
Exact phrase to tell a taxi driver when you want them to pull over right there.

kana: まどがわ、おねがいします
note: For Shinkansen or flights—say 通路側 (tsūro-gawa) if you prefer the aisle.

kana: していせき、あいてますか？
note: Shinkansen has 指定席 (reserved) and 自由席 (unreserved)—during holidays, always check reserved!

english: Can I top up my IC card here?
kanji: ICカード、チャージできますか？
kana: アイシーカード、チャージできますか？
note: Suica, Pasmo, and ICOCA work nationwide—convenience store registers can top them up with cash too.
Honest, clear opener before showing someone Google Maps or an address on your phone.
Handy when pointing at a paper map or asking a local where you are.

kana: あるいてなんぷんですか？
note: Gets you a realistic walking estimate instead of a vague 'it's close.'
Quick check before deciding whether to walk or grab a taxi (swap 近い for 'Is it close?').

kanji: チェックイン、お願いします
kana: チェックイン、おねがいします
note: Walk up to the hotel/ryokan front desk and say this with your passport or ID.

kanji: 荷物、預かってもらえますか？
kana: にもつ、あずかってもらえますか？

beats.jp: 預かってもらえますか？
beats.kana: あずかってもらえますか？

note: Most hotels and ryokans happily hold your bags for free before check-in or after check-out.

english: Until what time is it open?
note: Handy for shrines, museums, hotel breakfast, or onsen hours.

kanji: ここはどこ行きですか？
kana: ここはどこいきですか？
note: Great at confusing multi-route bus stops.

english: Is it okay to take photos here?
kanji: ここで撮ってもいいですか？
kana: ここでとってもいいですか？
romaji: Koko de totte mo ii desu ka?
note: Temples, shrines, and small shops often have no-photo areas—asking first shows huge respect.

english: Could you take a photo of us?
kanji: 写真、撮ってもらえますか？
kana: しゃしん、とってもらえますか？
note: Polite way to ask a stranger to snap a photo of you and your friends.
Omiyage (individually wrapped regional snacks) are huge in Japan—bring a box back for coworkers or neighbors!
Pure joy after soaking in a hot spring.
Works for an onsen soak, a cool summer breeze, or a shoulder massage.

kanji: 空港まで、お願いします
kana: くうこうまで、おねがいします
note: Clear instruction when hopping into a taxi.
Warm reflection with friends on the train ride home.

english: To each their own / Everyone's different
note: A smooth, non-judgmental way to wrap up a debate about food tastes, lifestyles, or opinions without disagreeing directly.

english: It'll work out somehow / We'll figure it out
note: Slightly more dramatic than なんとかなる—used when you're in a bind and trusting things will fall into place.

english: It'll work out / We'll manage somehow
note: The default everyday way to say 'It'll work out somehow'—more common in casual speech than どうにかなる.

english: What a waste! / Too good to waste
note: Used when food is thrown out, talent is wasted, or someone skips a great deal—and also in まだもったいない ('Too good to throw away yet').

english: We're even / We're in the same boat
note: When someone apologizes or thanks you for something you also do (like both being late or helping each other out), this says 'Hey, it goes both ways!'
Praises someone when they live up to their reputation (e.g., a friend who speaks great Japanese or knows the best hidden ramen spot).

english: I knew it! / Just as I thought! / After all
note: Classic reaction when a hunch turns out right—say やっぱり！ with friends, or やはりですね politely.

english: No way! / You don't say! / Surely not!
note: Playful shock ('No way! / Don't tell me!') when something wild or unexpected happens.

english: It's just your imagination / Probably nothing
note: Reassures a friend who thinks someone is mad at them or heard a weird noise.

english: Not bad at all / Pretty decent
note: Casual thumbs-up ('Not bad at all!'). Careful using it toward elders or someone's home cooking—it can sound slightly lukewarm.

english: That was really helpful / Good to know / Learned a lot!
note: Way more natural than ためになる—say 勉強になりました to mentors/elders and 勉強になった！ to friends.

english: My hands are tied right this second...
kanji: 今ちょっと手が離せなくて…
kana: いまちょっとてがはなせなくて…
note: Trailing off on なくて… is how locals smoothly say 'Sorry, I'm tied up right this second!'

english: So busy my head is spinning!
note: Literally 'my eyes are about to spin'—use this when work or errands are crazy hectic.

english: It has real charm / character (vintage, cozy bar, etc.)
note: Praises cozy vintage character (an old kissaten, a hand-painted sign, a weathered bar)—don't use it for food flavor!

english: Does it suit your taste? / Do you like the food?
note: Often asked by hosts or bartenders (お口に合いますか？)—great to recognize when someone checks if you like what they served.

english: Doesn't ring a bell / Doesn't quite click for me
note: Literally 'doesn't go *ping!*'—super natural for 'Doesn't ring a bell' or 'Doesn't quite click for me.'
Quickly lets someone off the hook after teasing them.
Tone matters! Said playfully it means 'For real?!', said flatly it sounds confrontational—use マジで？ for softer surprise.
Strong, natural 'Unbelievable!'—works for both amazing news and shocking surprises.

english: It was meant to be / Funny coincidence / Good fate
note: 縁 (en) is the Buddhist idea of fate/connection—sweet thing to say about a lucky coincidence or meeting.

english: Can't be helped / Nothing you can do
note: Same vibe as しょうがないよ ('Can't be helped')—just a tiny bit softer.

english: Thanks to you, I'm doing well
kanji: おかげさまで、元気です
kana: おかげさまで、げんきです
note: The classic humble Japanese reply when someone asks how you've been—literally 'Thanks to your support, I'm well.'
Polite 'After you!' at elevator doors, train doors, or checkout lines.

english: I'll be careful / I'll watch out
note: Polite promise ('I'll be careful!') when someone warns you about icy steps, late trains, or overworking.

english: Eh, whatever / Good enough / Never mind
note: Even more casual than まあ、いいか—a cheerful shrug when you decide not to sweat the small stuff.

english: What time is it right now?
note: Put すみません in front when asking a stranger on the street or at a station.

kana: さんじにおねがいします
note: Clean way to book a table, haircut, or clinic slot—watch out: 4 o'clock is よじ (yo-ji), 7 is しちじ, 9 is くじ.
半 (han) means 'half past'—super fast shorthand when confirming meetup times with friends.
Quick way to ask when a cafe, gym, or shop opens every day.
Classic same-day text to a friend to see if they want to grab dinner or drinks.
Quick check on whether tomorrow works for someone.

english: How about the day after tomorrow?
note: Great word to know: 一昨日 (ototoi = 2 days ago), 昨日 (yesterday), 今日 (today), 明日 (tomorrow), 明後日 (2 days from now).

kana: こんしゅう、いそがしい？
note: Friendly opener before asking someone to hang out this week.
Way more natural with friends than textbook 来週、会いましょう.

kana: せんしゅう、いきました
note: Clean past-tense update—swap 行きました for 行ったよ with friends.

english: What are you doing this weekend?
note: Easy Friday small talk at work or with friends.
Clear way to explain when a schedule, sale, or class kicks off.

english: Closed on Sundays / Off on Sundays
kana: にちようびはやすみです
note: You'll also see 定休日 (teikyūbi = regular closed day) on shop signs—many local restaurants close one weekday!

kana: ひとつ、おねがいします
note: Japanese native counters (ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ) work for almost any physical object up to 10.
Handy at bakeries, street stalls, and cafes when pointing at items in a glass case.

kana: みっつ、おねがいします
note: Same native counter series for 3 items—just hold up 3 fingers too if it's noisy!
Japan is super solo-dining friendly—walk into almost any ramen shop or cafe and say ひとりです.
Remember: 1 person = ひとり, 2 = ふたり, 3 = さんにん, 4 = よにん (never しにん!).
Keep this casual for friends—add ください (５分だけ待ってください) for couriers or drivers.

kana: じゅっぷんくらいです
note: くらい (kurai) means 'about / roughly'—super useful for time estimates.

kana: いちじかんかかります
note: かかる (kakaru) is the go-to verb for how long something takes (and how much fees cost!).
Polite update when texting a coworker, client, or host that you're almost there.
Punchy reply when a friend asks 'When did you get here?' or 'When did that happen?'

english: They were here just a moment ago
note: さっき means 'just a little while ago'—handy when someone asks if a coworker already left.

kana: いつでもだいじょうぶです
note: Polite 'Anytime works for me!' when scheduling an appointment or delivery.
Polite ask before picking up a delicate item at a craft shop or browsing a display.
Japanese shop clerks greet you enthusiastically when you walk in—this politely says 'Just browsing, thanks!'
Say this before heading into the fitting room—clerks will usually hand you a face cover so makeup doesn't get on shirts!

kana: エムサイズ、ありますか？
note: Sizes in Japan often run one size smaller than US/EU sizes—always worth trying on!

kana: ほかのいろ、ありますか？
note: Japanese stores often display only one color on the rack and keep the rest in drawers or the back.

kana: ちょっとおおきいです
note: Swap 大きい (big) for 小さい (chiisai = small) when asking for a different size.

english: I'll take this / I'll buy this
note: Clear, simple signal at a boutique or market stall when you've decided to take it.

english: Do you have more in stock?
note: 在庫 (zaiko) is 'stock/inventory'—useful when the display model is scratched or your size isn't on the rack.

english: Please put them in separate bags
kana: ふくろ、わけてください
note: Handy at the konbini or supermarket when you want hot food separated from cold drinks, or gifts bagged separately.
Japanese department stores and bookstores often do gorgeous free gift wrapping if you mention it's a gift!
Price tags now usually show tax-included (税込), though wholesale and some menus still list pre-tax (税抜).
Quick check on clearance racks.

english: What time are you open until?
kana: えいぎょうじかん、なんじまで？
note: Or ask politely: 何時まで開いてますか？ ('Until what time are you open?').
Popular bakeries and ramen shops often sell out before closing—you'll also see 完売 (sold out) on signs.
Open a photo on your phone, show a clerk, and say これ、探してます—works like magic in hardware stores and drugstores.

english: Could you wrap this for me?
kana: つつんでもらえますか？
note: Polite follow-up after saying プレゼント用です ('It's a gift').

kana: ゆうびんきょく、どこですか？
note: Post offices (〒) are everywhere in Japan and also have ATMs that work reliably with foreign cards!
You can buy postage stamps at konbini registers as well as post offices.

kanji: アメリカまで、お願いします
kana: アメリカまで、おねがいします
note: Clear at the post office counter—swap アメリカ for any country.

english: How much for sea mail vs. airmail?
kana: ふなびんとこうくうびん、いくら？
note: 船便 (funabin = sea mail, 2–3 months, cheap) vs. 航空便 (kōkūbin = airmail, fast). Also EMS for tracked express!

kanji: クリーニング、お願いします
kana: クリーニング、おねがいします
note: Japan's neighborhood dry cleaners (クリーニング) are super affordable and fast—often ready in 1–2 days.

english: Around when will it be ready?
note: Useful at dry cleaners, shoe repair, glasses shops, and photo printing.

kana: りょうしゅうしょ、おねがいします
note: Unlike a regular register receipt (レシート), a 領収書 is an official stamped receipt for business expenses.
Clerks love exact change in Japan—say this as you hand over the coins!
What staff say to you at cafes, boutiques, and ryokans—means 'Take your time / Make yourself comfortable!'

english: For now, this one / Let's start with this
note: とりあえず ('for now / first things first') is one of the most-used words in Japan—especially とりあえずビール！ ('Beer to start!').

english: I really appreciate it, but... / Hate to turn it down, but...
note: せっかく acknowledges someone's kind effort or a special occasion—makes turning something down feel genuinely appreciative.

english: Since we came all this way!
note: Classic justification for getting dessert, staying another hour, or visiting one more shrine ('Since we came all this way!').

english: Even so, that's a bit too much / Honestly, no way
note: さすがに means 'even considering everything / honestly'—great for pushing back gently on a wild idea or long walk.

english: I kind of get it / Have a vague sense
note: なんとなく ('somehow / kind of / without a specific reason')—locals use it constantly when they can't pinpoint why.
意外と ('more than expected / surprisingly')—sounds super natural when something turns out better than it looked!

english: I have a feeling that's true / Seems like it
note: Softens an opinion into 'I have a feeling that...' instead of sounding overly certain.

english: It's not like that / Not necessarily
kanji: そういうわけじゃない
kana: そういうわけじゃない
note: Essential nuance clarifier: 'It's not that I dislike it / It's not like that.'

english: It won't work anyway / No point trying
note: どうせ ('anyway / in the end')—casual, slightly dramatic way to say 'Eh, it's probably not happening anyway.'

english: Thought so / Just as I figured
note: Confirms your hunch ('Yeah, I figured as much!').
Soft, realistic agreement when something isn't ideal but makes sense.
Super natural spoken pivot ('Or actually, if anything...') when refining what you just said.
とにかく ('anyway / first of all') cuts through overthinking and gets everyone moving.
そろそろ ('soon / about time') is the gentle Japanese cue to wrap up a hangout or leave for the train.
Handy when you're 5 minutes from finishing work, a walk, or a beer.

english: That worked out great! / Perfect timing!
note: Warm reaction when timing, weather, or seating works out in your favor.

english: I'll go ahead and take care of it (in advance)
note: -ておく (-oku, often contracted to -とく) means doing something in advance so you're set for later.
-てみる (-miru) means 'try doing X and see what happens'—makes requests and offers sound light and natural.

english: I went ahead and bought it!
note: Casual contraction of 買っておいたよ ('I went ahead and bought it in advance!')—super natural with roommates or friends.

english: Yeah, that's the thing / Right, I know
note: Warm, relatable 'Yeah, that's the thing, right?'—shows you really get where they're coming from.

english: If I had to pick / More on the ... side
note: Great when asked 'Are you a dog or cat person?' or 'Coffee or tea?' → 'If I had to pick, more on the ... side.'

english: It was just a coincidence / By pure chance
note: Handy when you bump into someone on the street or nail a lucky shot ('Pure coincidence!').
Soft sigh of acceptance ('Guess it can't be helped').
念のため ('just in case / to be on the safe side')—makes you sound super thorough and considerate.
Warm, casual 'Huge help!' when a friend sends a link, holds your spot, or lends a hand.

kana: さいきんバタバタしてる
note: バタバタ is onomatopoeia for footsteps/papers flapping—the #1 way locals say 'Life has been crazy hectic lately.'

english: Hanging in there / So-so / Taking it steady
note: Originally Kansai dialect, now heard everywhere—means 'So-so / Hanging in there / Moving along.'
Locals love this word—said for old songs, childhood snacks, or neighborhoods you haven't visited in years.
Describes an awkward silence, running into an ex, or saying the wrong thing.
Friendly 'I'm jealous!' when a friend is going on vacation or eating somewhere amazing.

kana: めっちゃきょうかんする
note: 共感 (kyōkan) is empathy/relatability—great when a friend vents and you feel the exact same way.
Natural reaction when a friend tells you about a brutal commute, rent hike, or strict boss.
-すぎる (-sugiru) means 'too much'—so 無理しすぎないで gently tells a friend 'Don't burn yourself out.'

kana: のみほうだい、ありますか？
note: Most izakayas offer 90- or 120-minute 飲み放題 (nomi-hōdai = all-you-can-drink)—often pays for itself in 3 drinks!

kana: ラストオーダー、なんじ？
note: Izakayas usually call last order (L.O.) 30 minutes before closing or before your 飲み放題 timer ends.

english: What is this starter dish? (izakaya table charge)
note: At most izakayas, お通し is a small automatic appetizer that acts as a seating/cover charge (usually ¥300–¥500)—it's not a mistake on your bill!

english: Put 'Customer' on the receipt (blank recipient name)
note: When you ask for an official expense receipt (領収書), staff will ask 「お宛名は？」 ('What name should I write?'). Saying 上様で tells them to write the traditional generic placeholder instead of spelling out your name.

english: I need a certificate of residence
kana: じゅうみんひょう、ほしいです
note: You'll need a 住民票 (residence certificate) at the ward office for leases, banks, and driver's licenses—you can also print it at konbini with a My Number card!

kanji: 住所変更、お願いします
kana: じゅうしょへんこう、おねがいします
note: Every time you move in Japan, you have 14 days to update your address at the ward office (on the back of your residence card).

kana: こうしん、いつまでですか？
note: 更新 (kōshin) applies to visas, apartment lease renewals, and driver's licenses.

kana: ふりこみで、おねがいします
note: Bank transfers (振り込み) at ATMs or online are still how rent, clinics, and many local services get paid in Japan.

kanji: 引き落とし、できますか？
kana: ひきおとし、できますか？
note: Auto-debit (口座引き落とし) saves you from paying utility bills by hand at the konbini every month.

kana: いっかつで、おねがいします
note: Store clerks often ask 「お支払い回数は？」 ('How many installments?') when you hand over a Japanese credit card—always say 一括で ('All at once!').

kana: てすうりょう、かかりますか？
note: Japanese ATMs charge ¥110–¥220 outside regular weekday hours—worth checking!

kana: あんしょうばんごう、わすれました
note: Banks and ward offices lock your card after 3 wrong PIN attempts, so don't guess!

english: I want to ask your advice on something
kana: ちょっとそうだんしたい
note: Warm, respectful way to ask a friend or coworker for advice on life, work, or relationships.

english: So thoughtful of you! / You're on top of things!
note: Huge compliment in Japan—praises someone who notices small details and thinks ahead for others.
Warm praise when a friend nails something effortlessly ('Classic you!').

english: I've been curious about this place/thing forever!
note: Great thing to say when you finally try a cafe, neighborhood bar, or movie you've had on your radar.
Simple, happy wrap-up on the train ride home after a great day out.
